newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Warplane bombs Kabul in Afghan night raid.
newsitem.headline: Warplane bombs Kabul in Afghan night raid.

text.p: A warplane dropped at least one bomb on Kabul on Saturday in the first night raid on the Afghan capital since the Taleban takeover a month ago, witnesses said.

It was not immediately clear who launched the raid. Both the Taleban and it foes, an alliance of former government forces under Ahmad Shah Masood and northern leader Abdul Rashid Dostum, have started using warplanes to bomb enemy positions.
The plane, flying low and fast over the capital under a full moon, sparked furious anti-aircraft and machine-gun fire from Taleban defenders, witnesses said.
Streaks of tracer fire swept the night sky after the raid, 15 minutes before the 9.00 p.m. to 5.00 a.m. curfew.
Taleban fighters were still firing 30 minutes later although it was not immediately clear whether the plane, or planes, had returned.
There were no immediate reports of casualties or damage.

After taking the capital on September 27 the purist Islamic Taleban advanced on Masood positions some 80 km (55 miles) north of the capital before being pushed back to a strip some 30 minutes' drive north of Kabul.
From these positions it has faced sporadic rocket fire on the airport and at least one bomb before Saturday night's raid.

Dostum, who has only recently committed his forces to the civil war between the purist Taleban and former government, sent two warplanes to bomb positions in a valley north of the capital earlier on Saturday.
Taleban warplanes have been bombing Masood positions in towns south of the Hindu Kush, including one raid on Thursday in which 14 civilians were killed.

Witnesses said they heard the plane fly over the city at 8.45 p.m. local time (1615 GMT) on Saturday, dropping at least one bomb and sparking furious salvoes of anti-aircraft, machine gun fire and at least one rocket.

Despite years of factional warfare which has destroyed whole swathes of the capital, Kabul has been comparatively free of fighting since the Taleban takeover. Masood has twice warned the Taleban to leave Kabul or face bloodshed.
The Taleban opened a new front in the war on Thursday by attacking Dostum's western flank in the country's remote northwest, apparently dashing any lingering hopes of a ceasefire among the factions.
